newsitem.title: USA: U.S. concern as Kabila nears power.
newsitem.headline: U.S. concern as Kabila nears power.

text.p: With power shifting in Zaire, there is growing concern in the United States about rebel chief Laurent Kabila, who has never governed a country and whose commitment to democracy and free markets is suspect.

Alleged massacres of refugees, Kabila's interference with humanitarian aid efforts and his decision this week to nationalise a key railway reinforce doubts about his ability to reconcile Zaire's fractured society and lead it into an era of peace and stability, U.S. officials and other experts say.
But as Kabila is the apparent victor in Zaire's civil war, it is with Kabila that the United States and the rest of the international community must increasingly deal.

"Mr. Mobutu's reign was terrible. What is coming could even be worse," William Shawcross of the International Crisis Group, a non-profit organisation that monitors humanitarian relief, wrote recently in the New York Times.

U.S. officials are almost as pessimistic. "There are no good options for all the countries that are looking into Zaire ... We must accept reality," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said recently.

The United States, like France, must also accept a large measure of responsibility. It was intensely involved in resource-rich Zaire for three decades, boosting Mobutu as an anti-communist ally with millions of dollars in aid.

According to a report by analyst Jean-Claude Williame and others, Washington took no initiatives to suggest a willingness to break with Mobutu until recently when rebels came to control most of Zaire and Mobutu's power was disintegrating.

"In fact, both the Bush and Clinton administrations were partly paralysed in their search for new credible political actors in Zaire, being highly suspicious of the radical opposition," the report, published by the U.S. Institute of Peace, said.
Mobutu, stricken with cancer and with rebel forces poised to take Kinshasa, left the capital on Wednesday, ostensibly for a regional summit on Zaire's civil war.
Aides insisted the veteran leader, who has dominated Africa's third largest country for over three decades, would return from the summit in Gabon by Friday.
But many Zairians -- and U.S. officials -- said they did not expect him to ever come back. "If he comes back, it's at great risk," one U.S. official said.

Now the U.S. focus is on trying to persuade Kabila -- who in the past preached Marxism and in the 1970s took Americans and others hostage -- to pursue democracy and a free market economy in resource-rich Zaire.

U.S. officials acknowledge Kabila is little known to them. "He's proven picky and difficult in the runup to (South Africa-mediated peace talks with Mobutu last weekend) and he's been a real sphinx since ... Nobody's really quite certain how this guy's going to act or react," one U.S. official said.
Washington has been calling, with no result, for urgent talks between Kabila and Mobutu, or Mobutu's representatives, so when rebels enter Kinshasa a bloodbath does not ensue.
Despite reassuring statements, it is not clear Kabila will let Kinshasa change hands peacefully, U.S. officials say.

The administration, uneasy about Kabila marching unimpeded into the capital, has also pushed him to agree on a transition government that would include other members of the political opposition, like Etienne Tshisekedi, who was jailed years ago for opposing Mobutu.
U.S. officials admit Kabila, with his military might, could ignore this demand and may have reason to because Tshisekedi is popular and could represent a political threat to Kabila.

But defying Washington could be costly. "If Kabila does play ball with a transition government and it includes Tshisekedi, then the West will deal with him," one official said. U.S. aid in rebuilding Zaire will depend on Kabila's willingness to pursue democracy, free markets and elections, he and other officials said.

Many analysts were encouraged that Bill Richardson, U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, was sent to the region last week to demonstrate intense and high-level U.S. engagement and deliver strong messages to both Mobutu and Kabila.

Now, says David Schorr of Refugees International, a relief group, "the challenge is is in the follow-through." Thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees have died during the onslaught by Kabila's Tutsi-dominated rebel alliance and Kabila "has a hell of a lot of explaining to do as he comes into power," he said.
"When we're dealing with this problem, we have to keep in mind Kabila's pattern of assurances and broken promises."
